# 1. First approach to the unitary system by virtue of which a model can be considered scientific  

## 1.2 Delimitation of the scientific from the unitary character of some specific elements in the model

In any pictorial representation it can be devised a communication between figure and background, and many times the entire picture takes the name the figure has, as in Leonardo Da Vinci's Last Supper. It also happens in some cases that the name of the painting is given by the context over any figure that can stand out, as in Rafael Sanzio's The School of Athens. In science, what names the model? It stands out, after quickly recalling some examples such as the atomic model, the double helix model of DNA or the Hicks-Hansen model in economy, that the models, at least some of them, seem to be bottomless figures!

As a first attempt to clarify this fact, it is now suggested that it is not to the model that this character of bottomless figure should be attributed, but to a particular aspect of the model, namely its unitary structure. Thus outlined, the thesis sounds: a model is scientific only if it contains what will be called a unitary system, also called pattern from now on, such that a unitary system or pattern is an arrangement of unitary elements, also called concepts. It remains to be clarified whether this characteristic, which is proposed as being both necessary and the most relevant, is as well sufficient to consider the scientific character of models.

A suitable starting point or first approach to begin to understand a unitary element of which (as suggested) every model is composed, if scientific, is to think of such element as a bottomless figure, for example "mass", "time", "investment–​​saving", "DNA" and "ecosystem". If this is difficult to understand at first impression, it is for one reason only: it is too obvious. The adage is fulfilled once again that what seems the farthest is actually the closest. High school students are able to learn the difference between a particular distance (for example the distance between the chalkboard and the door) and the distance in general terms; or the difference between x meters measured and "the meter"; or between their teacher and the human being.,

It is not idle to clarify that numbers fall within this characterization of the concept in terms of unitary character of elements, and that the relationship between the conceptual unity in general and the number 1 is not of identity nor is it unproblematic either. For now it is enough to take into account that all models that are based on quantitative relationships, like in general physical models are, have their unitary system manifested in these relationships themselves, and also, very importantly, that these are not the only ones: there are models that are not based in numbers not even as a possibility and this does not exempt them from achieving a unitary system or pattern, which means: from being scientific models. Therefore, it is proposed to keep the term “unity” for general explanations and let “unit” for the particular case of numerical context.

Here it is worth adding that unitary elements need not to be assumed as empty entities all identical to each other, as mathematical entities could be thought to be, but each one has its own identity, its proper characteristics, announced by its name (the concept of "penguin" is not the same as the concept of "meter") and shaped largely from its relationship with other elements. Thus, a penguin drawn in a webpage will be different from “the penguin walking on the beach of Punta Tombo we saw last Thursday”, and this conceptuality difference is mainly given by the limited relationship that the first has with some specific elements of the drawing and its explanation on the webpage, in contrast with the countless multiplicity of relationships of the second in its natural habitat.

The consideration of the pattern as a unitary system embedded so to speak in the model (and correspondingly, as it will be make clear soon, in the target) may allow a highly conciliatory midpoint between the structuralist view, whose analysis must be thus thought as restricted to the isomorphic relationship between both symbolic and empirical patterns, and the model-based view, which is interested in the epistemology of the whole model and its relationship with the whole target. A study of the first with some detail has its place in section 6, while the second will be addressed mainly in section 2. Regardless, the influence of these two main currents can be strongly appreciated in the entire essay.

The term system is used in this study almost as a synonym for structure. Strictly speaking, a structure as an arrangement of unitary elements is part of a system, which also has a dynamic with unitary rules for causally or temporally modifying its structure. For example, causation can be considered an outstanding rule that has the effect (worth the redundancy) of individualizing the passage from one structure, or from one structural element to another, thus becoming time itself unity. Thus understood, the differentiation between system and structure can be tricky, since if such rules are unitary, then they fall as elements of a structure, and ultimately it cannot be said that in this case there is anything other than structure. This is not completely true, since, as it will be seen below in section 1.4, real conceptual systems are never composed of unitary elements with such a specification that they can be thought of as univocal in their unity. In any case, the term system fulfills its function of drawing attention to the intrinsic dynamic power of the unitary structure of the case.

According to this, the appearance of concepts may well be thought of as a first distinctive mark of the scientific, but, it must be now admitted, by no means sufficient. Indeed, all institutional disciplines handle concepts, no matter how alien to science they may be. A religious institution, for example, may well handle concepts such as "church", "grace", "prayer". And yet, it can be said it is not scientific because there is not, and it cannot be projected as a possibility a conceptual system for its object, for example among the historical episodes of its sacred text. Fortunately for the Jews and for their faith, the relationship between Abraham, Isaac, mount Moriah, and God is not unitary in the sense of necessary, otherwise what would become of Abraham's glory earned by his blind devotion to God? The essence and value of the religious is not conceptual, although each of the four above mentioned can well be said to be concepts for believers, in the specified sense that concepts are understood as relatively free from a multiplicity of contextual relationships and therefore elevated in their understanding. The relationship between them is not in turn unitary, and thus highlights the distinctive character of science: in allowing systems composed of a unitary multiplicity of concepts, as will be explained in more detail in the subsections below. Now, can it be said that the conceptual system is the sufficient element to explain the scientific and its difference from the non-scientific? The answer is no, but this is all that can be said about it in the symbolic domain. In section 4 this topic will be touched upon again when it comes to the empirical domain of science, and it will be seen that, in order to advance in an idea of demarcation, the intimate relationship with technology is crucial.

  
  

## 1.3 Constitution of the pattern of the model based on a process of conceptualization

  

Please consider the following quote of the ISO 704 standard (Sec.5.1) concerning the nature of concepts:

  

In communication, not every individual object in the world is differentiated and named. Instead, through observation and a process of abstraction called conceptualization, objects are categorized into classes, which correspond to units of knowledge called concepts, which are represented in various forms of communication (object → concept → communication).

  

There is, according to this ISO terminology, "a process of abstraction called conceptualization" which divides the waters, on one side "every individual object in the world" and on the other side "units of knowledge called concepts" in which "objects are categorized into classes". For any object in the world to be categorized, it must first go through a process of conceptualization.

The relationship between objects and concepts is not immediately evident in the cite, so it may need some clarification. Concepts are not directly accessible to knowledge but only through objects that reference them. When a scientist is in front of an animal (an object) and calls it "penguin", s/he categorizes it as a case of the penguin concept, which is not accessible except through objects that share the characteristics by which the scientist identifies them as penguins, or through the term "penguin", spoken or written, which is also an object. Such a term is part of the symbolic system, while the respective animals are part of the empirical system represented by the former.

The first sentence in the cite states that an individual object in the world can be differentiated and named. What does differentiation mean here? Is the object undifferentiated with anything else before being conceptualized? This topic is extremely complicated and it is very easy to get entangled in a series of arguments that do not lead, as it is intended here, to achieve something clean. Attending this warning, it will simply be said that, beyond the discussion on the differentiation between one object and another, what is interesting, as has been suggested in some paragraphs above, is the general differentiation between the object and its context—assuming that all other objects are part of the context. Understood in this sense, the conceptualization process, according to the ISO 704 standard, consists (presumably among other things) in differentiating the object from its context.

Does the object just become a concept once delimited from its context? Or rather is it grouped into a set associated to the concept (for example, object C belongs to the conceptual set of objects C)? Herein it will be chosen to interpret the object / concept as a token / type relationship. This relationship is not free from internal debates, but it has the advantage that precisely because of the fruits of these debates it is mature enough to be taken for the present purposes without further harm. In particular, it will be assumed that the types (concepts) are not exactly "in" actual tokens (objects) but in the possible tokens. The concept of "table" has its instances, which are particular tables, and the concept makes sense not as long as there are tables, but as long as there is the possibility of having any table. From this clarification it is understood that for example the phlogiston was a concept that made sense while the scientific community maintained the intention of getting a model that includes it as a component of atmospheric air. Once oxygen was established in the canonical models to explain the phenomena in question, the phlogiston became a meaningless concept outside its historical value.

The site also says that concepts are represented in various forms of communications. Please read the following extract from the same section of the Standard ISO 704, as interesting and rich as the first:

  

The concepts contextualized in the special language of the subject field can be represented in the various forms of human communication according to the system used. In natural language, concepts can be represented by terms, appellations, definitions or other linguistic forms; they may also be represented by symbols; in artificial language, they can be represented by codes or formulae, while in multimedia they can be represented by icons, pictures, diagrams, graphics, sound clips, video or other multimedia representations. Concepts may also be represented with the human body as they are in sign language, facial expressions or body movements.

  

So far there are objects disposed of in the realm of the empirical, and with this quote communication is posed in the realm of the symbolic. How do both interact? According to the aforementioned clarification in the first quote (object → concept → communication), the link between the two is the concept. It should be noted that what the ISO Standard calls concepts are directly the unitary elements as they are being introduced in this section, and that is why they can also be called conceptual unities, or directly, concepts. Therefore, it remains to clarify how the concept (unitary element) acts as a link or bridge between the empirical and the symbolic.

A great advantage of observing and highlighting the unity into the model is that its relationship with its counterpart in the target is also unitary, and this is certainly an indispensable condition for the unitary (conceptual) system of the model to make sense. Thus, from the main thesis the following corollary follows: although it does not make sense that the model is identical to its target (since it would not be a model but a copy, an imitation) their respective patterns (unitary system) must tend to be equivalent, otherwise the model does not exceed its scientific claim.

Whereas in section 5 a full detailed case study is practiced, for now one example may suffice so that the same simple and basic logic can easily be applied to any scientific model, since, again, it is extremely usual for any scientist or science theorist. Suppose a model to explain the water cycle in a given region has the following concepts or unitary elements: a mountain, a river, a lake, clouds with a certain concentration, an underground channel through which water moves, the atmosphere and water in certain concentration depending on their state. The model could be much more complex and complete, nothing prevents it from being so. It should also be clarified that it will necessarily contain other non-unitary elements that will help constitute the whole of the model. But now it is interesting to highlight these unitary elements in their interaction and affirm that the model makes sense iff there are things, in the place assigned as the target, which serve as objects for each unitary concept of the model: there must be a mountain with the characteristics that the model has considered relevant to survey, a river, eventually clouds, etc., and all interacting homologously to how the corresponding concepts interact in the model. This could be not the case, and then the model is just wrong since it represents a possible target, but in this case not real nor realizable. The criteria for evaluating models from this account is thus subordinated to the in-practice criteria that scientists have for evaluating models in general.

  

![](data:image/png;base64,)

  

The San Francisco Bay Model could be considered a similar, just that more complex case, in which its designers have had to detect, or perhaps decide, from the real bay those relevant (unitary) elements to carry out the construction of the model. The risk of all this is, again, that it is not understood because what is being said is too obvious and well known.

  
  

## 1.4 Specification gradation between the pattern and the annexes within a well-conceived model

  

Regarding the relationship with the pattern and the rest of the elements in the model, which can be called annexed elements, it is worth taking into account some clarifications. On the one hand, the relationship between the pattern and the annexed elements is not expected to maintain the unitary degree observed (or alleged) for the relationship between the elements of the pattern (intra) or the elements between patterns (symbolic / empirical). There is no sense in searching for general rules between unitary and annexed elements, and indeed the scientific nature of the model does not depend on it. Only in the most mature cases can a pattern be at least clearly differentiated from its annexed elements. On the other hand, annexed elements are not expected to present surrogative character—they are not expected to necessarily help represent something in the target. Correlatively, annexed elements in the empirical pattern are not expected to have corresponding elements in the model.

The above arouses a warning. A hasty reading of the Standard ISO 704 could lead one to consider that there is in a model a marked distinction between the pattern and, besides, other elements called annexes. This would not be strictly true. In no case it is a question of meeting or not the goal of achieving a pattern, or in particular in getting or not getting the conceptualization of a unitary element. Rather, it is found that scientific progress consists of gradually reaching a pattern for each subject. For this, it is judged convenient now to introduce the concept of specification to express to what extent a concept has reached a unitary character in the sense described until here. It is understood that in a model the pattern consists of elements with greater specification with respect to the annexed elements. Still, even in the best of cases it is not convenient that the distinction between pattern and annex is sharp, since then the connection between both would become quite incomprehensible. Furthermore, even within the pattern it is convenient to be prepared to find elements that are highly specified than others.

In physics, the concept of energy is much better accomplished than in cognitive sciences is the concept of intention, for example, or that of the namesake concept of energy outside of physics. When a cognitivist says “intention” s/he must necessarily clarify what s/he is particularly understanding by it. When a scientist says energy in the context of classical mechanics anyone who knows this subject understands what s/he is talking about, for "energy" is associated with a limited number of other concepts, several associated at the time with numbers. The term “energy” may also be, as the case may be, associated with a multiplicity of annexed elements, but the established models of classical physics allow the pattern to be distinguished with sufficient clarity from the annex. The well-known fact that a concept achieves its unitary character much better if it is related to numbers, and above all with numerical parameters that allow this concept to interact with other concepts through a mathematical formula, has an explanation that unfortunately is out of the scope of this presentation, although this is a conclusion presumed to be uncontroversial. The role of mathematics in science is a central theme that should not be underestimated in any respect.

It also follows from this that the sharp division between scientific models and models that are not cientific is not correct. It does make sense, on the other hand, to analyze how specific the pattern of a particular model is, in order perhaps to evaluate possibilities to improve its design based on this fact.

The semantic set-theoretic view of theories (to be studied in some detail in section 6.1), submitted to the recent conclusions, seems to have the same problems as the so-called syntactic view, which are based on the truth value of their postulates. If the latter maintain a sharp criterion between true and false, and as long as the former maintain a sharp criterion between what is and what is not part of a set, then they both will deviate, due to this rigidity, from scientific practice, but this does not means that scientific practice is a undesirable deviation from an optimal state to which science should have. No, the wide polar annex-pattern gradation in the specificity of the elements within a model is part of the best possible conception of a scientific model rather than a precarious state that will be overcome when the models are exclusively composed of absolute conceptual elements.

One point that may be controversial in view of the specificity of gradation is the claim that it is very difficult, if not impossible, to measure or dimension such gradation and define the specificity of each element. Certainly, all measurement is possible thanks to a prior establishment of a conceptual system, as will be seen in section 4. First of all, it is worth taking into account that such measurement is in no way necessary nor is it even necessary to establish a hierarchical non numerical scale between the most specified elements and the least within a pattern. For the purposes of philosophical evaluation of a model (but not for the purposes of design and use of a model) it is interesting to detect the unitary elements that make up the pattern in broad strokes. Even this specification does not require marked precision, and this is due to gradation itself: any excessive precision in defining the pattern of a successful model must be a liar. But neither should one fall into the conclusion that everything does not matter. The consensus in the scientific community on the elements that are relevant in a model is a very valuable criterion for detecting these elements and should not be neglected, but it is certainly insufficient. After all, what leads the community to a consensus at once is nothing other than the successive and iterative results of measurement and observation. Indeed, measurement cannot establish the "measure" of the specification, but it can indicate that the specification has been on the right track. The anchor for the establishment of a model and its pattern is then not in the model, nor in the target, but in their interaction. Explaining how measurement in science is responsible for exerting this effect is the challenge that has guided the section 4, which is dedicated to this topic.

  
  

## 1.5 The permanence principle applied to concepts and the cluster as an outstanding composite concept

  

The increasing specification can be translated, according to what has been said so far, into an increasing reduction of noisy-elements with which the specified element is potentially bounded, up to a point where the resulting concept is only mostly associated with other concepts. A direct consequence of the establishment of a concept is what can be called the permanence principle. The fact that an element loses its relationship with its context does not mean that from then on it is prohibited by some constraint to approach it. Rather, it must be understood that, even being together with a (weakened) multiplicity of other elements, the concept is not modified by them. So this, far from preventing its presence in certain contexts, allows it to be precisely present in a multiplicity of contexts without being modified by them for the sake of a permanence principle, and the limit of the permanence of a concept (how long or how many times it remains through variation in its context) is determined each time by those elements that it has not been able to get rid of, or by those other concepts with which it is related to by its very constitution. For example, the number associated to a (variable) parameter in a mathematical formula will be prone to being modified based on the other variables in the formula, and in general the variation of everything else (such as the material support on which the formula is written, the scientist who writes it, the country, etc.) does not affect it.

It must be admitted that mathematical elements offer extreme specification cases for which the factors that limit the invariance of a concept can be countable and the imposition of the ceteris paribus clause makes sense. The study of the behavior of an animal in its natural habitat is another no less scientific example, although it shows a gradation between elements that directly modify the object of study and an increasing multiplicity of elements that modify it sporadically and unpredictably, with which the principle of permanence is expressed very differently, and instead of a ceteris paribus clause there would be better to think of something like a ceteris paribusness degree of the concept in question. To be clear: the permanence principle defines the existence of a concept and marks a limit between science and non-science, but in turn this limit has not scientific objectivity but its objectivity is uncontrollably gradual, and it is neatly false that everything that it does not arrive at the individuation that is own of the mathematics falls outside the orbit of the scientific.

Everything that has been said regarding the relationship of a concept with other elements of its context is valid to evaluate the relationship of a concept with its constituent elements: its specification reduces its intrinsic complexity to a point where this element can be described mostly from its constituent elements, also turned into concepts. This is how the ideal gas law, for instance, is made up of the concepts P, V, n, R, T, *, =, and also PV=nRT is itself a concept. The same happens with the ammonium molecule, which is composed of N and H, and also NH3, as a concept, is what determines its relationship between the formers. Likewise, lichen is a concept that contains the concepts of fungus and algae, each with its constituent concepts.

Here there is no point in claiming a system of concept orders containing concepts to arrive at some meta-scientific formalization that could certainly never be adapted to the variety of intra- and inter-relationships between concepts found in existing scientific models. It may be preferable to accept, as a given fact, that concepts have their own physiognomy and, depending on the model in question, may or may not be composed of other concepts. The possibility of containing concepts in concepts also reduces the formal characterization that is usually done for set-theoretical accounts, which generally states a set of elements plus a set of relationships between elements. In this case, the second set is no longer necessary, since the relationship between concepts is given by its particular place in another concept that contains it. On the other hand, because of what was said in the previous section on the gradation between the pattern and the annexes, there is no point in trying to specify the pattern as a concept made up of its elements. 

That a composite element, when conceptualized, is released from its context and thus becomes a bottomless figure, it means that its relationship with any other element that has not been as well conceptualized is weakened. There are times when the composite concept reaches such a specification that it can even become independent of other concepts within the pattern. But the process of cleaning a concept with respect to other elements until it is possible to specify, also in a unitary way, an exclusive relationship between a discrete list of their constitutive unitary elements, is a teleological aim to which scientists tend in the successive design of models. In such a limbo one could think of a relatively limited set of unitary elements with absolute specification that, being only connected to each other, can only define each one from the others. This constitutes a tautological state of the resultant composite concept, and the concept that is closest to this state is called cluster, in which each element is defined mainly from the other elements within the structure.

A cluster is a composite concept that has reached such a level of specification with its constituent elements that it becomes autonomous with respect to patterns, and therefore is susceptible, by the permanence principle, of being related to multiple patterns without undergoing substantial modifications. Just as the permanence principle announces that a concept, by becoming independent of its context, begins to be able to relate to a multiplicity of elements without being itself modified, so also the cluster that becomes independent from the other elements of a pattern can be related with a multiplicity of patterns without being substantially modified. Although an exhaustive review of the concepts usually handled in science that are close to the idea of cluster will not be carried out here, it can be advanced that, in physical sciences, laws, principles and axioms are clusters, while in biological sciences stereotypes are clusters.

The cluster becomes stronger the less it includes little conceptualized elements, which, on the other hand, it does not seem to be able to do without. Certainly, if an array of conceptual elements can only be fully defined each exclusively from the others within the same group, this array would not have the possibility of being inserted into a model, since for this it will need to be related to annexes elements, and this same relationship breaks inevitably the purity of the definition of each unitary element. This is the reason why an absolute specification is not feasible, and the unitary character of the elements, even participants in a cluster, can never become strictly universal nor strictly immutable. Newton's first law appears to be a fairly close case to this, since Force, Mass and Acceleration interact with each other into the law so that each parameter makes sense from the other two. But not in such a way that it prevents them from interacting with others, for example with the constant 2π and the variable L in a simple gravity pendulum T = 2π√Lg.

Finally, it should always be remembered that the unitary system as the pattern and in particular the cluster could not be conceptual digressions that float in the air of the symbolic regardless of the empirical, but, if they are systems that give entity to the scientific, must always show a symbolic-empirical character, and necessarily have their counterpart among the verifiable facts. Thus, a cluster is a structure that, rendered in a whole model, has the power to un-render or show an embedding aspect of the natural called the target and make it its isomorphic unity pattern.

  

## 1.6 Causality, explanation and prediction in terms of unitary elements

  

- Lo que se ha llamado predicción en ciencia se puede entender en los términos aquí propuestos como un sistema de conceptos que por su misma conformación dan lugar a un concepto que hasta el momento no venía siendo reconocido como tal. La metáfora del rompecabezas es adecuada en este caso, si se piensa en un conjunto de piezas que completan una sección de un gran cuadro tal que dejan un espacio rodeado o circunscrito en el que puede encajar una pieza, en este caso el elemento que se predice.
    
- La explicación funciona como una dinámica inversa, pero con similar estructura: hay inicialmente una pieza que se quiere explicar, y las demás piezas conocidas se posan a su alrededor para darle sentido.
    
- La causalidad es en ambos casos la relación entre la pieza en cuestión y las que la rodean… más un detalle. Se suele situar del lado de las causas aquellas piezas que gozan de mayor generalidad nómica, y del lado del efecto las que gozan de menor generalidad nómica. Así, entre dos piezas aledañas, la más general será la causa de la más particular. Por eso se dice que la posición del sol junto con la altura del mástil son la causa del tamaño de la sombra, y no suele ser bien visto afirmar que la sombra es causa de alguno de ellos. También hay que tener en cuenta que no necesariamente dos piezas que se encuentran cercanas en un contexto deben ser relacionadas a la manera de causa/efecto. En el ejemplo, no hay tal relación entre la altura del mástil y el sol, que cada uno por su parte puede ser explicado en su contexto particular, con sus piezas aledañas según el caso. Se puede caer en esta clase de confusiones (menos propias de la práctica científica que de la especulaicón filosófica) si se intenta asumir estos términos como unitarios en el sentido de científicos, cuando no lo son. Pues no hay experimentos que anclen cieníficamente causas, ni explicaciones, ni predicciones.
    
- [esto no iría] Hay que tener en cuenta el corte temporal que ocurre en ambos casos: siempre hay un tiempo inicial, en el que quedan establecidas las condiciones iniciales o antecedentes, y un tiempo final, en el que queda establecido el resultado, la observación. Tal vez no hay otra alternativa que considerar siempre dos tiempos, inicial y final, y entonces la definición de causa se simplifica considerablemente: si un sistema en t1 siempre deriva en un resultado en t2, entonces el sistema es causa del resultado. Y causa no es entonces más que eso.
    

  

# 2. Ontology and epistemology of the scientific model as a symbolic differentiator of science

## 2.1 Definitions of the scientific model using the four Aristotelian causes

  

The definition of a scientific model stems from the difficulty that today there is not too firm a basis to define even a model in general. Dictionaries and encyclopedias coincide in that, in science, the meaning for the term model leans towards a device from which to represent what is generally called the target. Therefore, in science, a model makes sense as long as it is in relation to its empirical counterpart, a relationship called representation. This is also the starting point in this work, which has tried to advance a little more in the specification of the model by adding the pattern as a necessary component for it to be scientific. This leads directly to the possibility, but also to the need to define more specifically first the model, then the target, and finally the representation itself.

For the former, a strategy will be used to define what a scientific model is by resorting to a most time-honored tradition, the doctrine of the four causes, which it is assumed does not require an exhaustive introduction, and on the other hand its preference as a methodological decision should not cause any problems. For Aristotle, there are four causes that answer the question "why" about an object, in this case the scientific model: an efficient cause or principle of movement, a formal cause or essence, a material cause or matter and a final cause or end. In this case, the four causes of a given model will not be punctually practiced but will come to four definitions of what a scientific model in general is from the consideration of its four causes.

In all cases a scientific model is made from the need to understand nature conceptually and objectively, and to intervene on it. The scientist is the "agent" who has been trained for this task of understanding nature and, said roughly and in a very simplified way, the engineer has been trained to intervene on it from this understanding. Both scientists and engineers in their formation access the set of successive patterns and at the juncture they act to spirally generate new structures, complementing or revising the previous ones. This leads to the first definition:

  

Definition of the scientific model from its efficient cause: a scientific model is a device carried on by scientist and engineers in the attempt to understand and/or intervene in nature in terms of its pattern.

  

As there are multiple reasons that lead scientists to create models, there will consequently be a multiplicity of designs that give rise to “a proliferation of model types recognized in the philosophical literature. Probing models, phenomenological models, computational models, developmental models, explanatory models, impoverished models, testing models, idealized models, theoretical models, scale models, heuristic models, caricature models, exploratory models, didactic models, fantasy models, minimal models, toy models, imaginary models, mathematical models, mechanistic models, substitute models, iconic models, formal models, analogue models, and instrumental models are but some of the notions that are used to categorize models”. All these kinds are considered to share the aim of the "unitary understanding" of nature through a unitary symbolic system that is homologous to the empirical one in the garget, as introduced in the previous section, which leads to the second definition:

  

Definition of the scientific model from its formal cause: scientific model is any symbolic device that contains a pattern which can be verified in a homologous structure in the target from its representation.

  

If it has a symbolic character, what is ultimately a scientific model? What is its materiality? Recalling the second cite of section 1.3 from Standard ISO 704 can help to outline an answer.

  

In natural language, concepts can be represented by terms, appellations, definitions or other linguistic forms; they may also be represented by symbols; in artificial language, they can be represented by codes or formulae, while in multimedia they can be represented by icons, pictures, diagrams, graphics, sound clips, video or other multimedia representations. Concepts may also be represented with the human body as they are in sign language, facial expressions or body movements.

  

The lists do not need to be considered exhaustive to show that what defines a model as scientific is not indeed that it is made up of such and such material, or that it presents this or that other way or form of expression or, in short, that it has a specific support. It can be added: it is enough that it renders a pattern that can represent a homologous pattern in a given target. Thus, in view of the multiple material manifestations of a scientific model, the following conclusion is reached:

  

Definition of the scientific model from its material cause: A scientific model is any instantiation that renders the pattern attributed to a target.

  

Note that the meaning of this materiality does not exactly coincide with that of matter (mass) for classical physics. Instead, it means an instantiation of a formal order, which does not ask which elements a model is made of but in what way it serves as a channel to access our understanding. Thus, the matter / form pair can be thought to replace the concrete / abstract pair, most akin to being thought in relation to the material according to classical physics. For its part, the relationship between matter according to Aristotelian physics and matter according to classical physics will be further discussed below in section 3.2.

The fact that the pattern, which is formal, does not coincide with the model allows us to answer a series of questions that are turning in the bibliography about models and representation. One of them is the condition of directionality according to which representation does not prove in practice to be symmetrical and reflective (the model represents its object but not vice versa), as opposed to the conclusions that some accounts suggest, for example those that defend representation as similarity or isomorphism. Herein the problem seems to dissolve if it is considered that, although the pattern is always symmetrical and reflective at best, the complete model, always under a material aspect, is what relates to the empirical target in an unidirectional way, so that it can be asserted that the (entire) model represents its target in a scientific way iff it carries a pattern that is (symmetrically) identified with the one of the target. Strictly speaking, there is no representation between patterns.

The name given to the pattern serves as a methodological guide for the relationship between a model and the target. The name, indeed, is to be considered part of a material instantiation of the pattern. If it is about a model of the digestive system from a figure commented on a sheet, its name denotes that it contains the basic concepts of the digestive system (pharynx, esophagus, liver, stomach...) and that such unitary elements each have its counterpart in the body that the sheet represents. For the first definition concerning the efficient cause, it has been concluded that the conformation of a model is given by the need to understand nature, in the case of this particular example the human body, and eventually to be able to intervene on it. It remains to make explicit the final cause of the model, its specific purpose, the result of its use.

Considering its etymology, the term “model” comes from the Italian modello, broadly used during the Renaissance (XVI C), and this from the Latin modus, which can be translated as measure, size. In a music context, it is translated as beat, rhythm. Modus is also the root of other words such as modern, modify and module, that can be connected to “model” in order to semantically enrich it. It stresses the translation of modus as measure, which suggests that measurement is what adapts the model to something else. According to this etymological approach, a model can be thought of as something by virtue of which to measure (this definition broadly agrees with Morrison 2009, sec. 1). For the fourth definition of model, it will be often preferred to use the term “dimension”, since “measure” can be associated with the exclusively numerical. Thus, the term dimension admits numerical measure as a possible meaning, but is not restricted to it. Even with this caveat, it remains evident that the analysis of the measurement process in science, and through it, its interaction with technology, becomes indispensable to understand science from the particular view that is being proposed in this study.

  

Definition of the scientific model from its final cause: scientific model is each unitary arrangement from which it is possible to dimension an empirical target that allows for synergistic interaction with technology.

  

When analyzing scientific representation in theoretical terms, the scientific model is ultimately identified with the formal cause, while the target is generally identified with the material cause. This characterization has become in many cases a topic, since the publication of Giere´s (2004, 2010), who also talks about the need for subjects who design representation for certain purposes (efficient and final causes respectively). Such a proposal does not coincide with the one that is being attempted here, and this is not an indication of error in one or the other. In this section it has been preferred to focus attention on the model, which has shown to have a material character in addition to its formal structure.

  

## 2.2 Specification of the scientific model from a list of underlined characteristics

  

A series of characteristics that are considered typical of any scientific model are listed below, each attached with a minimal description. The set of these items is not intended to exhaustively describe the scientific model; each one has been selected above others because it is found more frequently in the bibliography and in its own way will allow to expand the characterization that is being attempted in this section.

Scale. It can be stated that all models have a determined scale; they have any proportion relation respect to their targets. Even it would be more direct to underline those models whose scale is 1:1 rather than specify the scale models as a type. Some models are recognized as “scale models” for maintaining their proportions in general terms with respect to those of the target. So scale models have unitary elements whose counterparts in the target have spatial dimensions that can be known from the spatial dimensions of the model element plus a conversion factor called scale, which, if numerical, maintains the unitary character of the relationship. In many cases the numerical relationship may not be so simple and direct (Sterrett 2019), but it must be observed that in any case the accuracy of the transformation is maintained, and this through the unitary nature of the elements involved in said transformation, at the risk of losing the desirable objectivity for any scientific model.

Analogy. Generally speaking, all models are somehow analogous to their target, since they are not identical and not completely different either; however, the name of the “analogical model” is generally applied to those models in which this characteristic stands out. Analogical models are those that have a pattern that is found not in the parts of a model, but in certain properties of these parts, or in other cases in the relationship between these parts. For example, in an electric–hydraulic analogical representation there is an "electron fluid" in a metal conductor represented through a water fluid in an hydraulic circuit. The water used is not in this case equivalent to electrons, but has properties that are objectively comparable to certain properties of electrons, such as flowing through pipes just as electrons flow through wires. The parts of the hydraulic model in the same way are not analogous to the parts of the electrical circuit, but they are arranged so that the properties of interest maintain a unitary relationship that always allows a unitary conversion between the model and the target. Thus, a simple pipe represents a conducting wire, a constricted pipe represents a resistance, a flexible diaphragm sealed inside a pipe represents a capacitor, a paddle wheel or turbine represents an inductor. But those are not the respective unitary elements that set the objectivity of the model, but their effects, as the particle speed of water with which it can be calculated the charge drift velocity, the direction of flow through a particular pipe and a respective wire, the water oscillating back and forth in a pipe representing the alternating current frequency and so on.

  

![](data:image/png;base64,)

  

Idealization. Without needing to enter into the discussion about what is and what is not ideal, or about what is an idea, models in general are considered idealizations in the sense that they dispense of a large number of (not unitary) elements that are present in the target. Those models that present this characteristic as distinctive and preponderant to carry out the representation of their target are usually made to fall under the category of “idealized models”. The proposal for the idealization of many historical models has given rise to controversy over whether it has been lawful to leave this or that aspect of the target aside. These controversies basically always consist of a specification of which the unitary elements of the model are finally and which are not. Idealization assumed in this sense, which is characteristic of all models in one way or another, always brings complications when the target is human behavior, as expected.

Fiction. This is a good answer to the question for the unitary system called pattern: it is a fiction. Each unitary element is a fiction, in the sense that it can only be accessible through what has been defined above as a material instantiation. It is said to be fictitious and not merely imaginary because, in addition, it always has (it is supposed) some resemblance to the objects that point to them. The concept "penguin", while, like any concept, relatively devoid of relations to its context, is not equivalent to any particular penguin, which is always only thinkable in a given habitat. But they both are undoubtedly similar in some respect, otherwise the concept has no possible practical application through that object. In general, “fictional models” are considered models whose conceptual pattern differs considerably with respect to the whole model, so the fictional character is underlined. Thus, a scale toy car will not be considered as hard as a fictional model since its pattern is relatively manifest and explicit in the model itself, but an atomic model represented by formulas will, since the pattern, composed for example by atoms, differs from the mathematical signs with which this pattern is expressed. Regardless, it is underlined, as in the previous items, that all models have a pattern that can be considered fictional, regardless of whether a model is (more subjectively) classified into the kind of fictional models.

Descriptive components. All models contain descriptions, either as the main component, or in addition to the main material component of the model. This is necessarily so because the pattern of the model must articulate with gradually less conceptualized elements, and nothing can accomplish this gradualness better than a descriptive explanation. It is not then a contingent issue that the explanation is always part of any model, be it a physical object, a graph or a formula. These, without an explanation, would have little to do in the context of scientific research and production. When the explanation also occupies the pattern of the model, such a model is in particular categorized as a “descriptive model”.

Exploratory potential. Models are not originally designed to reflect their pattern directly to that of the target, but to become so. When the pattern of a model agrees in an acceptable way with that of the target, the model has nothing to teach yet. To reach this state, a contrastation process is needed. The model originally presents a pattern with just some of their unitary elements already checked. Not all new unitary elements are always punctually checked, and it is up to each particular model to derive the criterion as to what extent a given number of contrastations allows to reflect the entire symbolic pattern to the empirical one. In general, the community accepts the model when a part of the new unitary elements has been checked, and while projecting the complete checking of the pattern it usually accepts the model as completely checked, which means that it is considered suitable for use by engineers. In general, when unknown unitary elements form a very relevant part of the pattern, the model is usually framed in the “exploratory model” class.

  
  

## 2.3 The precision frame for the model and its derivation on the discontinuity principle

  

Every measuring instrument has, by design, specified a maximum degree of precision that can be obtained when using it. With this precision degree the precision degree allowed by the model of a given object should not be confused. It is a fact that the precision of measuring instruments is related to that of the model to which the measurement results are directed, and when the precision of the instrument challenges the model, its credibility can go into crisis, as has been well noted by Kuhn (1979 The essential tension, el capítulo sobre medición). In any case, the measuring instrument must have a sufficient precision according to the precision required by the object model. Each model implies by design an upper and lower limit for the dimensioning of its target, such that outside the limits the same is no longer measured (Tal 2012). In the case of numerical models, the required precision is usually also suggested numerically; in other cases the precision is made explicit only when necessary.

Too much lack of precision makes the model stop being useful, but too much precision also does. Consider the example of measuring the coastal distance of a city by the sea (Weisstein 2008, Mandelbrot 1982). Due to the fractal nature of the coastline, the greater the precision in its measurement, the resulting distance will extend more and more until ridiculous extremes, so the model in question (for instance a map) must be designed, among many other things, considering an specification of the maximum precision point to measure the coastal distance —of course one that does not cover the effect of the waves and the tide on the coast. This is not an isolated example, a maximum limit for forming a precision frame is a constant for all models, and just as it is a common idea that everything qualitative, by being numerically framed, becomes quantitative, it must be considered with equal attention the fact that everything quantitative, when transcending its own frameworks (and it always have them), produces a qualitative leap.

Also consider the example of planetary models, and the maximum precision they impose on their design. It can be broken with the extreme simplification of taking each body as a geometric sphere and considering, for greater precision in the analysis of the case, the deformations of each one in particular with respect to a perfect sphericity, and even up to uneven terrain (such as large mountains) in a certain area of ​​its surface... but to what extent? Is it useful for the planetary model to consider the influence of the distribution of innumerable small rocks to calculate the trajectory of a certain planet around its star? Such a distribution may well serve in another model that deals with the specific properties of the planet's surface, and although both models represent the same planet, they should be considered non-continuous. This might be recognized as the "discontinuity principle" between models that share the same target and is a direct consequence of the precision frame that models always have by design.

The discontinuity principle imposes a self-limitation of models, and it is previous or a priory respect to the technologically-conditioned precision of the measuring instruments that are each time coordinated with such models. For the same can be concluded when it comes to direct observation: it is possible to make a model (it does not matter at this point whether it is scientific or not) of the shape of a mountain, when appreciated from a certain distance, in relation to the rest of the landscape the mountain is part of, and one very different model when being placed on such mountain, for example representing its typical flora. Both models will result in different "gestalts" of the same target, and could never continue each other. What would it be like to continue them? Would it be like beginning a drawing at a distance, continuing it as one approaches the mountain, and concluding it when one is on the mountain itself? It would be as much as drawing trees on a planisphere in the Amazon area pretending to complete it.

That two models cannot continue each other does not mean that they cannot communicate with each other: the unitary structure that is proper to science allows unitary elements to be made up of unitary elements, and this is what happens with models that are said to represent the same target: one is considered a structural part of the other. Thus, the pattern of one model on the surface of a planet is part of the planet that revolves around the sun as a conceptual unity in the other model. Similarly, the pattern of a model of a cell of a species of tree is considered a constituent part of the conceptual unity "cell", which in the pattern of a model of the tree can be only an element without much relevance. This kind of fractality that is characteristic of the conceptual unitary structure of science allows that two or more models that have the same target but not superimposed precision frames are both appropriate, although incommensurable.

  

Acá puede haber un error de concepto. No es que los modelos sean inconmensurables por sus patrones; al contrario, la intersección en parte de sus patrones es lo que los hace conmensurables justamente. Son los elementos anexos, su materialidad, lo que los distingue e identifica como modelos distintos.

# 3. Ontology and epistemology of the target as an empirical differentiator of science

## 3.1 First approach to the relationship between world and nature from a review of what is understood by nature

  

So far nothing has been said about the target except that it is a kind of system to which the model points within a scientific representation, and that somehow contains a formal element, the pattern, homologous to the respective model pattern. In case it can be granted for now that this is so, is the pattern in the target real? Is the relationship between the pattern and the target similar to that of the pattern and the model? Can any "portion" of the world or nature be liable to become a model's target? Again: is it possible to find a pattern for anything belonging to nature or the world? When something in the world is finally categorized into these unities of knowledge called concepts, that is, after going through a conceptualization process, is it still the same thing? What do we mean by “world” and by “nature”, in any case, such that part of them or something into them, or even themselves can presumably become the object of a scientific model?

Perhaps the reader agrees that in a first, to say a pre-analytical impression, the meaning of the term nature today seems to contain the knowledge established and recognized as scientific, while the term world can refer to the scope of everything known in general, including non-scientific knowledge, such as religious, artistic, social-political, etc, and even a pre-institutional or daily knowledge. If there was an agreement on this, is it necessary to state that nature and the world are two different "things"? Or that they mean the same but from different conceptual frameworks (namely, scientific Vs. not-necessarily scientific)? In any case, would an account that includes both in their difference be permissible? And if possible, is there any advantage to our understanding of science in targeting this distinction?

The very question about the difference between nature and the world seems to challenge, or at least generate a tension, with the naturalistic position, which in general affirm that there is nothing that resists being apprehended by science. Put the other way round, naturalism maintains that if something can be thought of that cannot be scientifically explained, such a thing is not real, or it is an imaginary invention or simply an error. If it is granted the strong naturalistic position that reality is exhausted by nature, there does not seem to be room to speak of the world as if it were something else that nature cannot achieve. But which is the concept of nature underlined by the naturalistic position of science in current accounts? Throughout history there have been many markedly different conceptions of nature, quite discordant with each other, and in each case it can be verified that the meaning given to the term depends on what it is contrasted with in each case. Next is suggested a rough list to highlight five of the main cases in which it can be noticed how each sense of nature carries with it a demarcation criterion for natural knowledge. The list is not intended to be representative of the term's multivocality; simply serve as a platform to suitable develop the theses of this section.

i) Nature(φύσις)  Vs. convention (or law, νόμος). Contrasting the natural with the cultural is a topic since Plato and the Sophists. Here nature has the sense of what occurs regardless of human purposes. For many centuries science assumed the semantic weight of this meaning, since the knowledge it claimed was about things as they are, which in this case means: prior to being modified by the human gaze. So naive, such a look of nature has been heavily criticized in the last century with the consideration that all access to things is always "loaded" with preconceptions, including theoretical.

ii) Nature (φύσις) Vs. artifice (τέχνη). Similar to the previous one, nature denotes the kingdom of all that has not been modified by the human, in this case it is about a tangible modification of the object. Here nature is the set of all those things that have not been changed by technique or technology (cf. Aristotle, Phys., II, 192 b, 18 for an early formulation of this distinction). Those things certainly still exist on Earth, for example in pristine jungles. Perhaps it is even possible to agree that it can still be scientifically known without being modified in its natural state. The question is whether something whose knowledge has been accessed with the help of artificial means can be considered natural in this sense, even without being modified in its natural dynamics, for example an in vivo mammal cell observed under a microscope. This topic will be further discussed in section 4.5 below. For now, it can be said that if observation is loaded with theory, understood not only as a theory that interprets and knows things, but also as a theory that modifies things, then, if indeed science and technology are essentially combined, as will be argued in section 4, the natural / artificial distinction suffers the same fate as the natural / conventional distinction of item i.

iii) Nature Vs. God. This meaning of nature as creature or “the created” ruled strongly during the Middle Ages. Here the meaning of nature takes a turn with respect to items i and ii in the sense that it is no longer something that simply happens (the prefix φύ- in φύσις means “that which emerges by itself”) in contrast to what “is happened” thanks to something else (said in general, conventions and artifacts occur thanks to the human projects). Instead, in this case is God “what” exist with independence of anything else and nature occurs thanks to “something” else —in this case God. Regardless of whether the efficient cause of nature is God or whatever else, the contrast with the previous versions of the natural is raised: on the one hand that which is independent of "external" intervention, on the other that which is given thanks to an intervention of any kind. It is of utmost importance for this section to visualize these extremes and understand the error of being posed in any of them, in order to start thinking a proposal that can get out of the dichotomy "immanent existence" / "transcendent existence", which does not mean to fall in a vacue midpoint that says nothing and simply takes refuge in a "deflated" place just to avoid being criticized.

iv) The natural Vs. the psychic. This distinction has its origin in the Cartesian distinction between res extensa and res cogitans, and was object of a remarkable debate in the middle 20th century (cf. Murphy 1945, Kim 2003) when the possibility of breaking it began to be considered, that is, considering whether natural (scientific) knowledge is able to encompass the scope of the psychic. This topic will be further discussed below in section 3.2. 

v) The natural Vs. the supernatural. This distinction is the one with the greatest force in the philosophy of science debates of the last decades, to the point that even the historical reviews of the demarcation in science sound convincing when performed with this key, and it has its raison d'être in the search to distinguish science from pseudoscience as a false, misleading and even dangerous knowledge. In every declaration of demarcation of this kind a Manichaean background can be noticed without much effort, but in this particular case the degree of moral rift and elitist claims that it supposes and advocates is embarrassing.

Insofar as the term naturalism expresses the yearning and even the effort to reach knowledge through the scientific method in areas where the scientific knowledge has not arrived yet, for example, the Human Spirit sciences (Murphy 1945, Kim 2003), one may not be a naturalist as long as one does not share this aim, but it is difficult to think of a non-naturalist who denounces the error of a search posed in such terms. If now the bet is redoubled and what is intended with naturalism is to cover, not other areas of knowledge, but all areas of knowledge, at least as a possibility, and hence naturalism becomes “the wholehearted acceptance of scientific method as the only reliable way of reaching truths about the world of nature, society, and man” (Murphy 1945), then it is no longer lawful to see as senseless the one who moves away from this premise. At least there exist conditions for a debate. 

If one agrees with the naturalist's proposal that there is nothing (as a possibility) that escapes an objective reading and scientific presumption, it is worth asking what happens to other possible ways of understanding the world and the things of the world. If the extension of the scientific becomes absolute, does it not immediately become exclusive as well? The answer is no, but neither should one rush to settle a resounding "no". It is true that the scientific knowledge of whatever does not disqualify knowing the same thing or things from another non-scientific, for example artistic, religious, etc. framework. It follows from this simple fact that a scientific framework can well encompass everything without the need to deny extra-scientific knowledge. There is just a small caveat to be drawn from this: perhaps it can not be an issue of law, for example a logical deduction, that other kinds of knowledge are very often too hidden behind scientific knowledge, but is a historical issue, perhaps of a sociological character. Then science itself is forced to observe its effects from a non-scientific path; science is the one that must set its own limits.

According to this, even when some form of naturalism can be acknowledged since there is in principle anything that cannot be known in scientific terms, it is also true that formalized language of science cannot encompass the richness of vernacular language, which transcends it, even when recognizing that science contains an ordinary language that has been just partially technified. In consequence, it is worth reviewing what it means that something can be scientifically known and at the same time it is known in a non-scientific framework; if one can speak of the same thing or in what sense “that” is understood as different things. It is in these terms that it is desired to propose in this section the terminological distinction between world and nature, the first encompassing the totality of what is known beyond science, and the latter encompassing the entirety of scientific knowledge. It is not, as it could be understood, two spheres that complement each other and could for example be represented with diagrams, but two ambits of knowledge, two categories, which are related as far as they refer to the same things, just that in a different way. Consequently, it is a matter now of focusing on understanding the relationship between world (the non-scientific) and nature (the scientific), since it seems that in this relationship a clue can be found to clarify much of what has been said about the demarcation problem in science.

A suitable starting point to begin to understand the relationship between nature and world may be from the classical distinction between episteme and doxa, being the former part of academic knowledge, while the latest refers to the knowledge of those who have not accessed a certain context that offers a special education. Contrasting epistemic knowledge with opinion is not the same as contrasting it with the quackery that is presumed competent to give qualified opinions, as Plato often did when referred to the Sophists. Sophism, in current terms, is rather assimilable to pseudoscience. It is the place not to be reached (as Hansson 2009, 240 makes it clear); doxa, on the contrary, is the starting point to be left behind on the path of formation.

Similarly, if nature is presented as a synonym of essence, then essence may be understood as the element that makes daily language rise above itself for the first time to achieve something like universality—said in the terms that are being used in this study, becoming a concept, reaching a certain specificity to be part of a structural object.

  
  

## 3.2 Brief discussion against physical materialism and some comments on truth and reality

  

Most authors seem to agree that naturalism is somewhat less naive than materialism since it concedes the existence of non-material entities, understood here “matter” from classical physics, not from Aristotelian physics as in section 2 it has been done. Naturalists just deny that these non-material entities have their own realization or that they depend on something other than the material (Nagel 1956, p. 7). Now, if science is only able to know material forms and their realizations and also a naturalist wants to evaluate the scientific with a scientific tone (Danto 1967, 488) this seems to bring a problem. As a naturalist will only evaluate a form of knowledge from the canons of scientific reasoning, he becomes incapable of valuing any form of non-scientific knowledge; therefore, he has no authority to disqualify it. He is thus obliged to confine himself in a cloister where it only can be known what he accepted, and forced by his method to deny the non-scientific at the same time as to ignore it. This, which thus described seems so improbable, is not the most usual thing in our days, where many philosophers simply assume themselves to be naturalists without believing that they need more arguments for this than their declaration? But defining naturalism from an already naturalistic position is at least a fallacy and leads to hopelessly tautological arguments. For example, the custom of opposing the supernatural to nature has turned out to be a bit misleading because it takes for granted the impossibility of accessing the supernatural, for it is out of the naturalist cloister, and thus leaves nature without margin with which to be defined or specified. Opposing the supernatural, often identified as deceptive and despised, often linked with immaterial spirits and souls, results in the comfort of contrasting a position with the worst of his otherness.

The mind / nature focus (see item iv in previous subsection) allows moving from the appeal to medieval monsters and dragons while going straight to the subject / object focus, a distinctive mark of modernity. In the relationship between the physical and the mental it is sought on the one hand to explain the mental with precepts that have historically served to explain the physical, and on the other to define the physical as the non-mental, with the strategy that the mind is just the non-physical. The problem with this is that it cannot be done without solving the former. If the mind cannot be explained in a reliable way, neither can the physical be delimited from the mental in a reliable way. And the truth is that today it has not yet transcended an explanation that frees us from thinking of the mind as something other than a chimera.

Despite everything said, if naturalism is susceptible to a complaint it is not from the demonstration of causal connections between the physical and the supernatural; such contrastation, would return that “supernatural” to something physical and naturalism would remain untouched; then its comparison with the supernatural is, once again, a misguided task. The true Achilles heel of naturalism is suggested to be seen in its clinging to the scientific conceptual system, not as the only valid one, but as a valid one. Again; It is not here a question of demonstrating the validity of another type of reasoning or belief, but of questioning that of physics: the myth of space-time-causation. This is certainly not the first time this is suggested, but its conclusion is perhaps original: that having buried naturalism as it is currently understood, physics will be redeemed and in general also the philosophy of science.

Let physical matter as a term proper to physics, without letting it transcend to the field of philosophy in the aim of explaining science in general. For this, an idea of matter as opposed to form, but also to the efficient cause and the final cause of that explained may be ultimately more convenient, as has been attempted in section 2. Then the pattern embedded in the target can be understood in a homologous way than the pattern embedded in the model that this target represents. Such a pattern is therefore the formal part of the target, which gives it a material support that, as with the model, does not need to share the pattern's universality characteristics. Therefore, just as the atomic model is far from being the model of a particular atom exclusively, and can be supported by a graph, a formula, a syntactic explanation, etc., in an homologous way, the structure of an atom such as this model manifests it can be found in multiple empirical objects. Representation in science, from this point of view, consists of a relationship between two material entities (the symbolic model and the empirical target) each with a respective formal system that tends to be identified in an isomorphic way, as it will be attempted to show below in section 6.

Despite the intimate connection observed between the conception of ​​nature in science and the problem of demarcation, and having being conceded also that the demarcation of science with respect to pseudoscience is erroneous as a claim, this reconsideration wave seems to reach with much greater slowness to physicalistic naturalism. Is it a rejection of the discussions of a metaphysical tone that makes so many authors assume this position, at least unreflective in public terms, in order to better dedicate themselves to other problems typical of the philosophy of science, as if the philosophy of science had to do with something else? A direct victim of this sinchado is the idea of ​​truth. If the limits of science are dissolved, then all claims to truth also seem to be dissolved—at least truth as opposed to falsehood (sophistry, pseudoscience). But this is not the case if an explicit or implicit physicalistic naturalism is maintained. And in all those cases where it seems that the fairly common factor is to assume both the demise of the demarcation plus physicalism at the same time, the idea of truth remains in a bipolar state in which it cannot be simply accepted but neither it is allowed to die.

Another victim is the very close idea of reality. In the multicolored variety of realisms that have arisen at this time this madness is evidenced. What idea of truth and what idea of reality is suggested that may fit with what is outlined in this essay? A truth and a reality not naturalistic in the sense of nature as opposed to falsehood and to the supernatural respectively, but pre-naturalistic in the sense of nature as contrasting to the world. It is the world, the non-scientific, the place of the real and the true, although both still irreflexive as such, which by specification science manages to make a unitary object. And so the reality and the true character of the scientific object are modified, only to the extent of its specification, as it will be seen hopefully clearer in the next subsections. If necessary, it can be called backward realism, by following Ratcliffe (2004) in their comments to Putnam. But how many philosophers of science are going to agree with the claim that reality is first of all what it is considered as such in everyday life, that is, among everything that is not scientifically proven?

All this invites to reflect that the inquiry about the reality of, say, H2O which we consider objective although we question its existence is not so relevant, nor the reality of the water we speak of when washing our hands, whose existence we do not question, although we do not consider it in objective terms. And that much more interesting to concentrate the research effort is the relationship between both, non-scientific water and scientific water, in order to finally be dismayed at the effectiveness of the verb “to be” saying, for centuries and absolutely effective, in any scientific context, that H2O “is” water.

  
  

## 3.3 The influence of the Democritean tradition and the Anaximandric tradition in western thought —including the scientific thought

  

Now, with full awareness that these topics are too important for the brief treatment that is being given in this work, whose main questions are certainly elsewhere, attention will only be drawn to a way of interpreting this issue in terms that in a one way or another, each time with their own features and in their context, there have accompanied the history of science and philosophy. It is about a contest regarding the search for truth that initially divided thinkers like Democritus and in some way Plato and Aristotle on the one hand and Anaximander, Empedocles and Heraclitus on the other. According to the first group (and once again the reader is asked for mercy for the child simplification with which this profound subject is being treated herein) the truth (and the real in a strong sense) resides in stable, eternal, universal, ideal, etc. conditions, and the tangible world, the world knowable by mortals, is a corrupted derivation of that sphere from which it falls figuratively but also ontologically. Thus, the truth to which the human accesses is partial and knowledge as an act is a movement (perhaps asymptotic) towards that which is perfect and immutable, which is thus established as a beginning (arkhé) and as an end (télos). The Cartesian tradition, whose influence is perhaps still the majority today in the philosophy of science, seems to be much closer to this “top-down” view and that is why the discussions on realism hover around questions such as to what extent the real can be accessed, or why such a goal cannot be accomplished. An extreme skepticism or anti-realism in this sense also falls on this side because they must assume the same point of view of the position that they deny.

For the other side of thinkers, that have had participants in history such as Hume and Nietzsche, the truth that man can access is the consequence of an emergency from chaos, the result of the configuration at first randomly from the unconfigured. Notably, this “chaos” can be as difficult to justify metaphysically as the “ideal” for the former authors. For both sides, télos can be thought to be roughly the same (objective knowledge), but here arkhé is, it can be said, opposite. Here there is no world of ideas from which the imperfect derives, but an Anaximander ápeiron from which what can be known arises. And therefore the idea of ​​truth as correspondence (homoíosis) is meaningless, since there is no ideal model from which to evaluate the false. Instead, the idea of ​​truth as unconcealment (alétheia) fits well. The truth in this sense is not understood in its contrast with its opposite, falsehood, but from the dynamic to unconcealment. All the philosophers of science who are recognized as pragmatists are much closer to this second sense of truth and from such a conception it is that they criticize the strong structuralist position—and this despite the fact that hardly anyone can argue that science lacks structure.

The present work intends to be inserted as well in the second, “bottom-up tradition", understanding everything known as unhidden (perhaps it is better understood as configured or assimilated from chaos or randomness), in a gradual process in which the movement towards configuration, assimilation or unhiding has been called specification (see section 1.4 above), and that scientific knowledge has greater specification in general with respect to everyday knowledge. It is worth clarifying again that in general all institutional knowledge is more specified and is more objective with respect to everyday knowledge; science also has a particular structure that allows it to be differentiated in some way from other non-scientific (objective) institutional knowledge (see section 1.2 above). As advanced in the introduction, there is no attempt here to understand the general question of the known out of chaos, but the movement from the everyday (just) known to the scientific known. For this reason it is framed as a philosophy of science and not of cognitive science, neuroscience or psychology study.
